paper.abstract: Teenagers use social media every day to negotiate identity and peer relations. This preprint version reports the same interview study of adolescent wellbeing online.

tion.
Methodology. We used a qualitative study design based on semi-structured interviews. Participants were twenty
adolescents aged fourteen to seventeen recruited through two secondary schools. Data source: interview
recordings, transcribed and analysed with thematic coding. The sample was purposive and the field data were
collected over one term. Each interview lasted about forty minutes and followed a topic guide on platform use,
friendships, and moments of exclusion. Methodology. We used a qualitative study design based on
semi-structured interviews. Participants were twenty adolescents aged fourteen to seventeen recruited through
two secondary schools. Data source: interview recordings, transcribed and analysed with thematic coding. The
sample was purposive and the field data were collected over one term. Each interview lasted about forty
minutes and followed a topic guide on platform use, friendships, and moments of exclusion.
Results. The main findings show that adolescents use social media mostly to maintain existing friendships and
to experiment with self-presentation. Key outcomes include a strong sense of belonging and occasional
pressure to respond quickly. Limitations

Social Media Use and Everyday Identity Work Among Teenagers. Abstract. This paper examines how
teenagers use social media to negotiate identity, peer relations and a sense of belonging. The research
objective is to describe adolescent experiences of wellbeing online. The contribution is an interpretive account
grounded in interview data. Introduction. Public debate about adolescents and screens often assumes harm, yet
the empirical evidence is mixed. The research question asks how young people themselves describe everyday
platform use, and what role it plays in friendships and self-presentation. Social Media Use and Everyday Identity
